rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Predict the products formed when \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) reacts with the following reagents : (Any two)
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}\) and then \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)}\)/Conc. \(\mathrm{HCl}\)
(iii) Tollens' reagent
rows.solution:
(i) WITH METHYLMAGNESIUM BROMIDE, then acid. The Grignard reagent adds its methyl group to the carbonyl carbon, and hydrolysis gives the alcohol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHOH}\)

The product is PROPAN-2-OL, a SECONDARY alcohol with one carbon more than the aldehyde.

(ii) WITH ZINC AMALGAM AND CONCENTRATED HYDROCHLORIC ACID — CLEMMENSEN REDUCTION, which takes the carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\):
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Zn(Hg)}/\text{conc. }\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_3}\)

The product is ETHANE. The Wolff-Kishner reduction does the same job in ALKALINE conditions, and the choice between them is made by whether the rest of the molecule can survive acid or base.

(iii) WITH TOLLENS' REAGENT. The aldehyde is oxidised to the carboxylate while silver ion is reduced to the metal, depositing a bright mirror:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + 2[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^+ + 3\mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COO^-} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\downarrow + 4\mathrm{NH_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is the ETHANOATE ION, the reagent being alkaline, together with metallic silver. A ketone gives no reaction at all, which is what makes this a test for aldehydes.

rows.stem: The resistance and conductivity of a conductivity cell containing \(0{\cdot}001\) M \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution at 298 K are 1200 \(\Omega\) and \(1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-4}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its cell constant and molar conductivity.
rows.solution:
The CELL CONSTANT is the ratio \(l/\mathrm{A}\) — the distance between the electrodes divided by their area — and it is found from the measured conductivity and resistance:
\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\left(\dfrac{l}{\mathrm{A}}\right)\), so \(\dfrac{l}{\mathrm{A}} = \kappa \times \mathrm{R}\)

Substituting:
\(\dfrac{l}{\mathrm{A}} = 1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-4} \times 1200\)

CELL CONSTANT \(= 0{\cdot}18\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

Then the MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY, with the factor of 1000 converting litres to cubic centimetres:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{\mathrm{C}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{0{\cdot}001}\)

\(\Lambda_m = 150\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The cell constant is a property of the APPARATUS, not of the solution — it is why a conductivity cell is calibrated with a standard potassium chloride solution before any unknown is measured, and the same constant then serves for every solution put in that cell.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
A reaction is first order in X and second order in Y.
(i) How is the rate affected on increasing the concentration of Y three times ?
(ii) How is the rate affected when the concentrations of both X and Y are doubled ?
rows.solution:
The rate law follows from the orders given:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{X}][\mathrm{Y}]^2\)

(i) Increasing \([\mathrm{Y}]\) THREE times, with \([\mathrm{X}]\) unchanged, affects only the second factor:
\(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = (3)^2 = 9\)

The rate becomes NINE TIMES its original value.

(ii) Doubling BOTH concentrations multiplies each factor by its own power of 2:
\(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = (2)^1 \times (2)^2 = 2 \times 4 = 8\)

The rate becomes EIGHT TIMES its original value.

The second result is simply \(2^{\,\text{overall order}}\), the overall order here being \(1 + 2 = 3\). Note that the EXPONENTS, not the coefficients in any balanced equation, are what do the work — order is measured, not read off the stoichiometry.

rows.subtopic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
rows.stem:
Predict the products in the following reactions :
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr} + \mathrm{CO_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_3CN} \xrightarrow[\text{(b) } \mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{(a) DIBAL-H}}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{H_3O^+}}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — In sub-item (iii) the reactant is printed as a DRAWN benzene ring (hexagon with alternating Kekule double bonds) bearing CONH2, not as a formula, over an arrow labelled H3O+ above and delta below. Sub-items (i) and (ii) are printed as ordinary formulas. The linear LaTeX in the stem is a faithful reading of that drawing and is corroborated by the marking scheme's answer (benzoic acid, so the ring is aromatic and the reactant is benzamide), but it is not what the page looks like, so the real crop should be attached. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
(i) A Grignard reagent attacks the carbon of carbon dioxide, and acidification frees the acid. The carbon count rises by ONE:
\(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr} + \mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COOMgBr} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

The product is ETHANOIC ACID. This is the standard way of lengthening a chain by one carbon while installing a carboxyl group.

(ii) DIBAL-H — diisobutylaluminium hydride — is a mild reducing agent that stops a nitrile at the IMINE stage, which water then hydrolyses:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CN} \xrightarrow{\text{DIBAL-H}} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}NH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)

The product is ETHANAL. The point of the reagent is that it STOPS there — lithium aluminium hydride would carry the reduction on to the primary amine.

(iii) Acid hydrolysis converts an amide to the parent carboxylic acid, the nitrogen leaving as the ammonium ion:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} + \mathrm{NH_4^+}\)

The product is BENZOIC ACID. The carbon count is unchanged, which distinguishes this from the Hofmann degradation of the same amide, where a carbon is lost and aniline is formed.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their property as indicated :
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\) (Reactivity towards HCN)
(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), \(\mathrm{Cl-CH_2-COOH}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-COOH}\) (Acidic strength)
(iii) Benzoic acid, 4-Nitrobenzoic acid, 4-Methoxybenzoic acid (Acidic strength)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Two sub-items are printed as drawings. In (i) the third and fourth compounds are drawn two-dimensionally as CH3 - C - CH2 - CH3 and CH3 - C - CH3 with the carbonyl O on a vertical double bond below the central carbon; the stem reads them as the condensed formulas CH3COCH2CH3 and CH3COCH3, which is exactly how the marking scheme writes them. In (iii) all three compounds are DRAWN benzene rings each bearing COOH at the top vertex, the second carrying NO2 and the third OCH3 at the para (bottom) vertex, printed in that order; the stem names them, which is lossless here because the question asks for an ORDERING and naming a compound does not state that ordering. Both readings are corroborated by the marking scheme (CH3COCH2CH3 < CH3COCH3 < CH3CH2CHO < CH3CHO, and p-methoxybenzoic < benzoic < p-nitrobenzoic). Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
(i) Increasing reactivity towards hydrogen cyanide:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO} < \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)

Nucleophilic addition begins with cyanide attacking the carbonyl carbon, so reactivity falls as that carbon is made less positive and more crowded — and every ALKYL group does both, releasing electron density inductively and blocking the approach.

The two KETONES come first, each carrying two alkyl groups, and butanone is the more hindered of them, its ethyl group being bulkier than a methyl. The two ALDEHYDES follow with one alkyl group each, and ethanal is the more reactive, its methyl group smaller than propanal's ethyl.

(ii) Increasing acidic strength:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}COOH} < \mathrm{CH_3COOH} < \mathrm{Cl{-}CH_2{-}COOH}\)

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the carboxylate anion. CHLORINE withdraws electron density by the \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect, spreading the charge and stabilising the anion, so chloroacetic acid is much the strongest — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 2.86.

Alkyl groups do the opposite, RELEASING density and intensifying the charge. The ISOPROPYL group releases more than a methyl, so 2-methylpropanoic acid is the weakest of the three — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 4.86 against acetic acid's 4.76.

(iii) Increasing acidic strength:
4-METHOXYBENZOIC ACID < BENZOIC ACID < 4-NITROBENZOIC ACID

The same principle, applied to a ring substituent at the PARA position, where its resonance reaches the carboxyl group directly.

The METHOXY group DONATES a lone pair into the ring, raising the electron density, intensifying the charge on the anion and WEAKENING the acid — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 4.47. The NITRO group WITHDRAWS, both inductively and by resonance, stabilising the anion and STRENGTHENING the acid — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 3.44. Benzoic acid itself, with neither, sits between them at 4.19.
